## Two kinds of aim {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**What I want you to understand**

- What reproducibility, robustness and replicability each mean, and why they come apart
- What open research makes available, and where it keeps it
- Why five analysts of one claim reached different verdicts
- What a reproduction needs besides the data and the code
- What a preregistration fixes, and what it leaves open
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**What I want you to be able to do**

- Find the data, the code and the registrations of a published study
- Write an estimand statement for a published claim
- Reproduce a recorded result exactly, and explain why it came out as it did
- Read a replication report against its preregistration
- Fill in a preregistration block before any result exists
:::
:::
::::

::: notes
Two columns, because the day has two kinds of aim. On the left is what I want you to understand, and today most of it is about open research: what the three kinds of repetition are, what open data, open code and registration make possible, and why even analysts who had the same open file did not agree. On the right is what you will have done with your own hands by the end: found the public record of a study, written down the question that its claim answers, reproduced a published number to the third decimal, and filled in a preregistration. None of that needs a statistics course behind it. The robustness exercise, in which you would vary the analysis yourself, belongs to another format of this course, and I will point to it at the end.
:::
